summary: A coordinate pair names ONE location on a grid with an ORDERED pair of numbers: the first tells how far ACROSS from the origin (horizontal, x-direction), the second how far UP (vertical, y-direction). Two ideas must be held together: the order is a fixed convention (so (2,4) and (4,2) are different points), and you read against the NUMBERED LINES from the origin (0,0), not by counting the squares. The most documented error is reversal — writing the vertical number before the horizontal. Coordinates are well supported by prior position vocabulary (along/across, then up) and grounded in the physical image of travelling from the origin — 'along the corridor, then up the stairs' — before abstracting to (x, y) notation. Activities below range from an interactive place-and-see grid, through diagnostic reading tasks, to static reveal scaffolds; each has a distinct purpose and its own limits.
misconceptions: Reversal — putting the y-coordinate before the x (reading/plotting up before across), giving an incorrectly placed point (documented, NCETM).
Believing the order is arbitrary — treating (2,4) and (4,2) as the same location.
Counting squares/cells instead of reading the numbered grid lines, producing off-by-one positions.
Not anchoring to the origin — starting the count at 1 rather than 0, or from the wrong corner.

activities.title: Coordinate-journey grid: place the point and watch the path
steps: Given a target pair such as (4,2), place the point on a numbered first-quadrant grid.
Watch the tool trace the journey from the origin — along 4, then up 2 — and drop the marker where you placed it.
If you read 'up before across', notice your point lands at 2-across-4-up, a clearly different point (a different gridline crossing) from the target (4,2), with the along-then-up trail showing why.
Press a compare control to drop (2,4) and (4,2) side by side so you SEE they are two different points.
Count against the glowing numbered lines starting from the origin (0,0), not the squares between them.
activities.insight: The order of the pair fixes the point — reading up before across lands you somewhere else — and counting is read from the numbered lines starting at the origin, not by counting squares.

activities.title: Read the point: diagnose reversal and off-by-one
steps: Read the coordinates of a plotted point on a numbered grid and write them as an ordered pair, e.g. (3,5).
Answer 'which of these is (2,4)?' with (4,2) also offered, choosing the correct point.
Match and name the coordinates of all vertices of a plotted shape.
Explain which number is 'across' and which is 'up' for each answer.
activities.insight: Reading a plotted point as (across, up) can be checked reliably, and a reversed or off-by-one answer indicates which misconception is likely at work.

activities.title: Labelled-grid reveal: seed the convention and the axis names
steps: Tap a point on a labelled grid to reveal its along-then-up reading (across first, then up).
Tap the x- and y-axes to reveal 'x = across, first number' and 'y = up, second number'.
Lift a flap comparing (2,4) and (4,2) to see they name different points.
Say aloud the rule 'x comes before y' and connect each axis name to its coordinate.
activities.insight: Each number in the pair has a fixed meaning tied to a named axis, giving a rule ('x comes before y') to fall back on when unsure of the order.

activities.title: Name the corners: coordinates as locations of a shape
steps: Read aloud the coordinates of every corner of a rectangle (or other shape) plotted on the grid.
Decide whether a point sitting on the up-line at height 3 with nothing across is (0,3).
Judge a claim such as 'B was written as (2,4), the same as A' when the grid shows A at 2-across-4-up and B at 4-across-2-up — show on the grid why it is right or wrong.
Explain how you remember which number comes first.
activities.insight: A coordinate is a single location, not two loose numbers; moving between a plotted point, a vertex, and the origin consolidates reading and justifies the order.

checkQuestion: Show a first-quadrant grid with numbered lines. Plot two points: A at 2 across and 4 up, B at 4 across and 2 up. Ask: 'Write the coordinates of A and of B.' Then: 'How do you decide which number to write first — and are A and B the same point or different?'
checkAnswer: A = (2,4), B = (4,2). The first number is how far ACROSS (horizontal, x) and the second is how far UP (vertical, y), counted from the origin (0,0); A and B are DIFFERENT points because the order matters.
